There are a lot of characteristics of a region in the southern part of the United States that make it hostile to the normal conception of a homestead.

In the local area, you have mostly rock-solid clay. That clay has a high sodium absorption ratio, which causes problems with many plants due to its alkalinity. We also have municipal water with too many dissolved mineral salts that affect the ability of plants to absorb water. The heat during the summer also kills a lot of plants regardless of what you do; many stop producing because they can't pollinate once the temperatures are high. This is why you will see many tomatoes stop producing in the summer.

Once you head away from the clay in the local area, you move towards soil with a looser texture that can support more plant roots, but the further west you go, the less rainfall you get. The more northeast you go, the more rainfall you receive. The further west and towards the low rolling hills, the more caliche outcroppings you encounter. Caliche is basically calcium carbonate and is hard for most plants. When you're buying land, sometimes there is a layer of soil a foot thick on top of caliche, which will be drought-prone soil that doesn't hold moisture well, so make sure you check. You can generally tell by the vegetation being shorter and more scrubby.

Towards a major city in the eastern part of the state, there is plenty of rainfall, and in general, the more rainfall a place gets, the more the soil shifts towards being acidic.

Many areas in the state also have radioactive well water, but no one will tell you that. There is a reason why there are so many uranium mines in this region.

With all that being said, if you find a place with a decent water well or other source, you can have tons of success as a homesteader. The biggest problem I see is that people get animals and heavily overstock their land. The carrying capacity in this general area is about one animal unit per 15 acres. The year-to-year rainfall availability changes the carrying capacity of the land, so you have to moderate your stocking density anywhere from 1 acre per animal unit in very favorable years to 40 acres per animal unit not even being enough in bad years.

You mentioned you would buy food, which means you can have more animals, but you will have to keep them contained and intensively manage when and how long they are allowed to graze in order to protect your pasture.

Don't just go through a property killing all the native plants because they are often edible, and you should learn about the native adapted edibles. Another thing is you should plant more adapted plants that aren't familiar to the average person but are used as food in similar climates in other parts of the world. An example is a local leafy vegetable that is actually one of the most nutritious vegetables on earth. Adapting your diet to what does well locally is the most important advice.

If you want to grow fruit trees, you need to use "low-chill" varieties. Temperate fruit trees need a certain number of hours per year below a specific temperature in order to induce fruit production. We don't get many of those hours anymore, so you have to hunt down varieties that only need less than 200 chill hours. An example would be certain apple varieties.
